summary: This section explains how a company's books and papers are handled after it winds up. The Tribunal decides how to dispose of them when the company is about to end. After five years, no one is responsible if these records are missing.
points: The Tribunal gives directions on how to dispose of the company books and papers when winding up is complete.
After five years from dissolution, nobody is responsible if a book or paper is missing.
The Central Government can make rules to prevent the destruction of these books and papers for a specific period.
Creditors and contributories can make representations to the Central Government and appeal to the Tribunal regarding these rules.
Breaking any rule or order made under sub-section three leads to a fine of up to fifty thousand rupees.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited completed its winding up process and was about to be dissolved. The Tribunal issued a specific order on how the company books and papers should be disposed of. Five years later, a former business partner asked to see an old ledger, but it could no longer be found. Because the five-year period had already passed, neither the former liquidator nor the person keeping the records was held responsible for the missing document. Meanwhile, the Central Government had created rules to protect certain records from early destruction, giving creditors the right to object if rules were broken, which carried a fine of up to fifty thousand rupees for any violations.

terms.meaning: A legal body set up to deal with specific disputes and cases.
The official closing or ending of a company.
The person appointed to wind up the affairs of the company.
A person liable to contribute to the assets of the company in the event of its winding up.

watch: People often confuse the five-year rule for keeping records with government rules that might require keeping them for a different period.
